qti-item-body.p: The collegium's singers perform from three-hundred-year-old part-books whose pages crumble at a touch, so age alone rarely slows them down. But a twelfth-century choir manuscript defeated everyone: square marks sitting on a four-line frame, following rules that no member of the ensemble had ever been taught.

A visiting specialist finally transcribed the archaic notation onto modern staff lines. Medieval singers once absorbed those square marks as naturally as children today absorb the treble clef, she noted, though centuries have passed since any working musician wrote music that way.

too difficult for anyone but a specialist to master

qti-content-body.p: The opening sentence removes this reading: the ensemble already performs from crumbling three-hundred-year-old books without trouble, so neither age nor fragility is what the word is doing here.

The specialist points out that medieval singers absorbed these marks as naturally as children absorb the treble clef — the notation was never inherently hard. Ask instead why no one in the ensemble was ever taught it.
The scale is wrong. The passage measures the gap in centuries, not in seasons or styles; reread the final clause of the passage and weigh what it says about the last several centuries.

Right. Age is not the obstacle here — crumbling three-hundred-year-old part-books are routine for these singers. What stops them is notation whose rules nobody is taught anymore, because working musicians stopped writing with it centuries ago.
Archaic means belonging to an earlier period of time and no longer in current use.

p.em: Much of his vocabulary felt archaic, so tied to his own century that Priya sometimes had to guess at his meaning.
In her grandmother's attic, Maya found archaic letters written in a spidery hand, words she'd never seen before because the language itself had changed so much.

qti-content-body.p: Archaic means something is not just old, but specifically old and no longer in use. It's more precise than "ancient" (which emphasizes age but not disuse) or "old" (which says nothing about whether the thing is still used). These letters belong to a vanished era of language — that's exactly what archaic captures.
